{"differential_diagnosis": [{"diagnosis": "Malrotation with midgut volvulus", "confidence": 0.95}, {"diagnosis": "Duodenal atresia", "confidence": 0.88}, {"diagnosis": "Jejunoileal atresia", "confidence": 0.75}, {"diagnosis": "Meconium ileus", "confidence": 0.72}, {"diagnosis": "Hirschsprung disease (early-onset total colonic aganglionosis variant)", "confidence": 0.62}], "diagnostic_uncertainty": 0.412, "reasoning": "Bilious vomiting and feeding intolerance since birth in a newborn are red flags for surgical gastrointestinal obstruction. Malrotation with midgut volvulus is the most urgent consideration—bilious emesis is often the first and only sign before ischemia or perforation; mortality rises sharply with delay. Duodenal atresia is highly associated with Down syndrome and typically presents with bilious or non-bilious vomiting and a 'double bubble' on X-ray; bilious vomiting occurs when obstruction is distal to the ampulla of Vater, which is common in complete atresia. Jejunoileal atresia causes variable obstruction depending on level; distal jejunal or ileal atresia frequently presents with bilious vomiting and abdominal distension. Meconium ileus—often the first manifestation of cystic fibrosis—presents with bilious vomiting, failure to pass meconium, and may show 'soap-bubble' or 'ground-glass' appearance on imaging. Hirschsprung disease rarely presents neonatally with bilious vomiting (typically in total colonic or long-segment variants causing functional obstruction proximal to aganglionic segment), but it is less common than structural atresias or malrotation and usually accompanied by delayed meconium passage and abdominal distension; confidence is lower due to lower pretest probability for bilious vomiting as a primary feature."}

Duodenal atresia is the most common cause of high intestinal obstruction in newborns and classically presents with bilious vomiting within hours of birth; it is strongly associated with Down syndrome and often shows a 'double bubble' sign on X-ray. Malrotation with volvulus is life-threatening and must be ruled out emergently — bilious vomiting is the cardinal sign, and delay risks bowel necrosis. Jejunoileal atresia typically presents similarly but may have slightly later onset or less consistent biliousness; however, it remains highly plausible. Meconium ileus (often in cystic fibrosis) causes distal small bowel obstruction and bilious vomiting, though meconium passage is usually delayed or absent — not yet confirmed here, lowering confidence slightly. Hirschsprung disease rarely presents this early with bilious vomiting (more typical in total colonic aganglionosis), and absence of meconium passage would be expected — but since meconium status is unspecified, it remains possible though less likely than the top four."}
